content.title: How Tennessee taxpayers can get an extension on April 15 taxes
content.text: Updated April 14, 2026, 9:52 a.m. CTTaxpayers can request a filing extension to October 15, but tax payments are still due by the original April 15 deadline.Some Tennessee residents affected by Winter Storm Fern qualify for an automatic tax filing and payment extension to May 22.The storm-related extension applies to residents in 23 specific counties, including Davidson, Rutherford, and Williamson.Affected taxpayers can also claim disaster-related losses and may receive waivers for fees on copies of previous tax returns.Did the April 15 deadline to file federal income tax returns sneak up on you?For those who aren't able to finish the paperwork in time, extensions are available with Internal Revenue Service Form 4868. To qualify for an automatic extension to October 15, the short form requires a name, address, Social Security number and estimated taxes owed or refunded. Importantly, the IRS extension does not apply to payments owed.Only the filing gets an extension, as tax payments remain due April 15.What is the federal tax extension for some Tennesseans?However, some Tennesseans also qualify for a tax filing and payment extension due to Winter Storm Fern in January, which caused widespread damages and power outages.For those living in eligible counties, the new tax deadline is Friday, May 22 — 37 days after the usual April 15 deadline.The IRS said the May 22 deadline applies to individual income tax returns and payments due on or after Jan. 22, 2026.Penalties for payroll and excise tax deposits due between Jan. 22 and Feb. 6 will be waived if payments are made by Feb. 6. The extension also covers affected quarterly payroll and certain excise tax returns due Feb. 2 and April 30.The eligible counties include:Cheatham CountyChester CountyClay CountyDavidson CountyDecatur CountyDickson CountyHardeman CountyHardin CountyHenderson CountyHickman CountyLawrence CountyLewis CountyMacon CountyMaury CountyMcNairy CountyPerry CountyRobertson CountyRutherford CountySumner CountyTrousdale CountyWayne CountyWilliamson CountyWilson CountyHow to receive Winter Storm Fern tax extension in TennesseeTennesseans who are qualified for the federal income tax extension due to Winter Storm Fern don't need to file anything, as the extensions are automatically applied to residents of eligible counties.The IRS will waive fees for copies of previously filed tax returns for taxpayers affected by the disaster. To request copies, taxpayers must write “Tennessee Winter Storm Fern” at the top of Form 4506 or Form 4506‑T before submitting it to the IRS.Qualified disaster relief payments are generally excluded from taxable income, allowing taxpayers to exclude money received for necessary living, funeral and home repair expenses.Taxpayers in federally declared disaster areas can also claim disaster-related losses on their federal return for either the year of the disaster or the prior year. Individuals have until Oct. 15, 2026, to make that election.To check a tax refund, taxpayers can use the IRS website, where information is typically available within 24 hours of filing electronically.The IRS issues most refunds in fewer than 21 days, especially for returns filed electronically with direct deposit.What happens if you miss the April 15 tax deadline?Penalties start to accrue immediately after the taxes were due if you don't file for an extension. Here's a breakdown of how it can cost you.The IRS willl charge a failure to file penalty if you don't file a tax return on time. The penalty is 5% of the tax owed each month, or for part of a month, the return is late up to a maximum of 25%. If your return is more than 60 days late, there's also a minimum penalty for late filing. The minimum penalty is the lesser of $525 this year or 100% of the tax owed.Additionally, failure to pay the full amount owed will further boost your costs. The IRS charges 0.5% for each month, or part of a month, up to a maximum of 25%, of the unpaid tax from the due date of the return until the tax is paid in full. The penalty increases to 1% if the tax remains unpaid 10 days after the IRS issues a notice of intent to seize assets.If that's not bad enough, the IRS also charges interest on any balance due. The interest rate is determined quarterly by the federal short-term rate plus 3% and interest compounds daily. In the first three months of the year, the rate was 7%.There is no penalty for filing late if you don't owe money or are owed a refund, but the IRS encourages you to file as soon as possible. If you're owed a refund, you can't get it until you file.USA TODAY reporter Medora Lee contributed to this story.
